transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-05
Start time: 16:30 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes
Attendees: Evan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Jon (Redwood SE); Alicia (Harborline Head of ML), Ben (Platform), Dina (Security), Mike (CTO)

Summary (auto): quick scoping for a 6-week POC to evaluate deployment modes and run throughput/latency benchmarks. Primary success criteria: P95 <= 200ms for standard inference path, sustained throughput 150 requests/s steady state, cost target under $0.003 per generated token equivalent, and SOC2+KMS compatibility.

[00:00] Evan Chen: ok thanks everyone for joining, A few intros — we're from Redwood, i'm Evan AE, with Maya and Jon on the infra side. Alicia: thanks, we really want to validate whether hosted will meet our SLA or if we need dedicated or private.
[00:28] Alicia Morales: quick context, Harborline runs an NLU layer for routing inbound B2B shipper messages, roughly 10k daily active users now, peak traffic bursts up to 400rps for short periods. Our main concerns are latency tail, PII redaction, and lock-step compliance with our provider KMS.
[00:57] Maya Singh: great. what's your current stack? are you using a managed endpoint or self-hosted models?
[01:12] Ben Carter: currently we run a mix — some Rasa + on-prem microservices, evaluation with a small GPU cluster for transformer features. We don't have a production LLM infra. We want to know cost and predictability tradeoffs.
[01:35] Mike O'Rourke: timeline is tight — execs want a recommendation in 6 weeks. ideally a POC that demonstrates latencies and cost, then decide on Dedicated reserved capacity or Private deployment.
[01:52] Jon Park: okay that aligns. for the POC we usually run a two-phase plan: Phase A bench for performance (throughput/latency/cost); Phase B run a privacy/infosec validation (KMS, audit logs, RBAC). For the performance bench we'll need representative payloads, sequence lengths, and concurrency pattern.
[02:25] Alicia Morales: yep we can share payloads. our average prompt length is 120 tokens, generation target ~40 tokens. Some calls produce 400 token outputs but that's rare. Also many requests include company PII in the user message which is why KMS and data retention are non-negotiable.
[02:48] Maya Singh: noted. for hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs: hosted gives fastest onboarding and the quickest way to test traffic under real conditions; dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput and private tenant isolation; private (VPC/on-prem) is best for strict data residency and HSM/KMS control. each has different benchmark tuning.
[03:13] Ben Carter: realistically our hurdle is compliance. Dina from security, want to jump in here.
[03:20] Dina Flores: sure. we need full audit logs, SSO/SAML integration, and KMS/HSM support for root keys. We also need a written data flow diagram for any POC runs. If the provider can't meet our encryption or log requirements, private becomes the only option.
[03:42] Evan Chen: understood. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and on-prem package. For POC we can simulate the private path by enabling a VPC-based private control plane and using customer keys — we can bring a test key for validation.
[03:58] Alicia Morales: that would be ideal if we can test both hosted and private-like flows during the same POC. what's the usual time to spin up dedicated capacity?
[04:12] Maya Singh: Dedicated lead time depends on capacity and region — typically 1–2 weeks to allocate reserved pool if we have availability, sometimes more for custom sizes. Hosted we can start ingesting traffic within hours. Private on-prem takes longer due to network and compliance — usually 3–6 weeks for full on-prem install, but VPC private control plane can be quicker.
[04:39] Mike O'Rourke: risk is if we do hosted and it's a mismatch, switching later has migration costs. can you quantify the migration effort?
[04:50] Jon Park: migration is mostly model pinning and routing changes — in practice it's a config and rollout procedure. For KV cache warmup and prefix caching there is some performance tuning when you move from hosted to dedicated because batching behavior changes, but we can instrument to keep results comparable.
[05:18] Alicia Morales: about success criteria — our product KPI is intent routing accuracy and latency. we want P95 inference <= 200ms for the 120/40 token pattern, and 99th <= 400ms under 200rps sustained. Also throughput target is 150rps sustained with headroom for 400rps burst. cost target standing is under $0.003 per token-equivalent, or roughly target monthly inference cost under $10k for initial rollout.
[05:53] Maya Singh: helpful. that's a clear set. we'll map these into the benchmark matrix. For benchmarks we'll run sweeps across model sizes (e.g., 7B quantized, 13B int8, and a 70B trimmed variant) and three batching strategies (no-batch low-latency, small-batch 4–8, and high-batch 16+ for throughput).
[06:18] Ben Carter: the 70B variant is more for quality checks; if we can hit latency on 13B that might be the sweet spot.
[06:30] Dina Flores: note we also need to confirm data retention — do you keep logs of full prompts? how long?
[06:38] Evan Chen: by default Redwood hosted keeps minimal telemetry and configurable retention. For POCs we can flip retention to the customer's desired window and show audit logs. For private, logs can stay inside customer environment or be forwarded to their logging endpoint.
[06:55] [07:00] Alicia Morales: also want to see how autoscaling behaves under burst — do you keep warm pools?
[07:06] Jon Park: Dedicated offers configurable warm pools and autoscaling policies. We can simulate realistic burst patterns in the bench. We'll include a test for cold start behavior and warm pool hit rate.
[07:26] Evan Chen: regarding cost modelling — we'll produce an apples-to-apples cost sheet comparing hosted per-token, dedicated reserved amortized cost, and private OpEx estimate. We'll include assumptions (avg tokens per request, cache hit rate, batching efficiency).
[07:43] Alicia Morales: excellent. how do you handle fallbacks if a model is temporarily unavailable? we can't fail our routing service.
[07:51] Maya Singh: Redwood has smart routing and fallback policies — you can configure lower-cost variants or smaller models as fallback with graceful degradation. We'll show a canary/fallback test in the POC.
[08:07] Mike O'Rourke: for security assessment, what artifacts do you need?
[08:12] Dina Flores: network topology, KMS integration details, identity maps for SSO, and any third-party subprocesses. Also the contract language around data ownership and audit privileges.
[08:24] Evan Chen: we'll bundle the security pack (SOC2, ISO docs), a sample network diagram, and the KMS integration guide.
[08:33] [08:40] Alicia Morales: great. on benchmarks — can you support running a 24h soak test to detect memory leaks or GPU throttling? We had issues in prior trials where 2–3 hour tests looked fine but long-run degraded.
[08:54] Jon Park: yes we recommend a 24–48 hour soak as part of Phase A extended run, especially for Dedicated and Private where thermal behavior can change. We'll include a long-run test in the matrix and provide logs.
[09:09] Ben Carter: what telemetry do we get? token-level latency, per-model token counts, KV cache hit rates?
[09:16] Maya Singh: we'll provide token-level latency histograms, per-route cost breakdown, cache hits/miss rates, GPU utilization, and tracing hooks for request-level debugging.
[09:29] Alicia Morales: perfect. next — workload sizing. our expected steady state by month three after rollout is about 150rps sustained with 30% average burst margin. Can you show a starting cost estimate for both hosted and dedicated?
[09:45] Evan Chen: yes we'll produce two scenarios: (1) hosted with dynamic autoscaling and caching tuned — estimate O($0.0025-$0.0035 per token-equivalent) depending on batching hit rate; (2) dedicated reserved pool — fixed monthly, which can be cheaper beyond a certain throughput (we'll show a breakeven). Private on-prem will be Opex + Capex and vary by infra choices. We'll put numbers in the sheet.
[10:09] Alicia Morales: we will want the breakeven analysis explicitly because finance will ask.
[10:14] Maya Singh: for that we'll need your expected 95th percentile concurrency and cache hit assumptions, that drives unit economics.
[10:21] Alicia Morales: i'll provide a CSV with traffic distribution and 7-day peak histogram.
[10:26] Evan Chen: perfect. for the POC schedule — given your 6-week decision window we propose: Week 0 (prep): share payloads and security artifacts; Week 1: hosted baseline bench; Week 2: dedicated reserve warm-up and bench; Week 3: private/VPC control plane bench & security tests; Week 4: 24–48 hour soak; Week 5: analysis and cost model; Week 6: exec review and recommendation. That fits the 6-week ask if we run some tasks in parallel.
[10:59] Mike O'Rourke: can you run hosted and dedicated benchmarks overlapping? we don't want to wait serially.
[11:05] Jon Park: yes some steps can run in parallel — for example hosted bench can run while we wait for dedicated pool allocation, and security validation can run parallel to performance bench. We'll mark dependencies in the timeline.
[11:16] [11:20] Alicia Morales: ok on data controls — one nuance: our legal team requires an encrypted-at-rest guarantee for any in-flight KV caches and that model training access is disabled for any PII. Does Redwood do that?
[11:33] Maya Singh: KV cache and runtime artifacts are ephemeral and can be set to never persist in hosted POCs; for Dedicated we can configure ephemeral caches and for Private the data never leaves your VPC. We can also sign a limited-use agreement for the POC.
[11:49] Dina Flores: we'll need a simple proof-of-concept that shows we can prevent storage of raw prompts.
[11:55] Evan Chen: we'll add a test to the matrix to validate non-persistence of prompts and show both the config and the audit log.
[12:03] Ben Carter: benchmarks — what tooling do you use for load generation?
[12:07] Jon Park: we use an internal harness and JMeter scripts for request shaping and a runner that can replay recorded traffic with exact timing and variance. We'll share the harness and the runbook.
[12:18] Alicia Morales: will you simulate real userthink times?
[12:21] Jon Park: yes we can replay 95th percentile, median, and burst patterns. We'll also include randomized long prompts to capture tail behavior.
[12:30] [12:35] Alicia Morales: thought about the model variants — if quality differences are marginal we might choose the cheaper 13B int8 path. Can you do automated qualitative evals tied to prompts?
[12:46] Maya Singh: yes we can run an eval set and produce quality metrics (accuracy, BLEU-like where applicable, and custom scoring). We'll include a small human-in-the-loop check for tie-breakers.
[12:59] Mike O'Rourke: for exec summary we need clear knobs: latency, cost, data isolation.
[13:05] Evan Chen: we'll provide a one-page rubric: success criteria mapping to pass/fail thresholds, and recommendation logic for hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[13:15] Alicia Morales: do you support HSM-backed KMS?
[13:18] Maya Singh: yes Redwood Private supports HSM integration; Dedicated can integrate with customer KMS where available; hosted supports customer-managed keys via API in some regions. We'll detail specifics in the security pack.
[13:31] [13:36] Alicia Morales: any gotchas about batch sizing that could surprise us? we've been burned by large batches increasing 99th latency unexpectedly.
[13:44] Jon Park: large batches increase throughput but can hurt tail latency — part of the POC is to sweep batch size and measure P99 under target concurrency. We'll include recommendations for dynamic batching thresholds.
[13:58] Evan Chen: also if you rely on prefix caching a lot, packetization matters for throughput — we'll instrument KV cache hit ratios.
[14:10] Ben Carter: what's the expected artifact set after the POC?
[14:14] Maya Singh: a bench report with raw traces, aggregated dashboards (latency histograms, token counts), cost model, security checklist, and a decision memo recommending hosting mode.
[14:25] Alicia Morales: perfect. last question — procurement: any standard enterprise terms we need to know?
[14:31] Evan Chen: we have enterprise SLAs for Dedicated and Private; hosted is standard TOS but we can append an SLA for accounts moving to paid tiers. We'll surface contract language as part of the follow-up.
[14:42] Mike O'Rourke: ok that's good. let's recap next steps.
[14:46] Evan Chen: recap: Evan to send benchmark template and example harness; Maya to propose test matrix; Alicia to send traffic CSV and latency targets; Dina to provide compliance contacts; Jon to schedule initial hosted run slots the week after next.
[15:02] Alicia Morales: thanks all. we'll aim to get the CSV and security docs by the end of the week.
[15:10] Evan Chen: great — we'll target the bench kickoff on 2026-12-14 assuming artifacts arrive.
[15:18] [15:20] Meeting ended.
